implementation_notes: In JavaScript the encapsulation unit is the module: a class in its own file whose helpers are non-exported module-scope functions, with its state in `#private` fields, needs nothing outside its own source to be understood. Private elements are hard private - no bracket access, no `Object.keys`, no reflection, no `JSON.stringify` - so callers cannot depend on internals even accidentally, which is what replaces the classic private-member structure; before ES2022 the same effect required closures or `WeakMap`, and those remain the fallback in older runtimes or for non-class (functional) code. Treat instances as values: expose operations that return new instances instead of mutators, and freeze where the language allows it.
pitfalls: Private elements are scoped to the class body and are not inherited: a subclass cannot see its parent's `#` fields, so inheritance cannot be used to extend a standalone class - compose instead.
Nothing prevents another module from monkey-patching the prototype: only `Object.freeze` (shallow) or a closure-based factory makes the type's behaviour read-only.
Private fields are skipped by `JSON.stringify`, `structuredClone` and `Object.assign`, so persistence and cloning must be explicit and callers cannot treat the object as a plain data bag.
Circular ES module imports initialise partially and silently, reintroducing exactly the dependency the class was supposed to avoid.
